transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump showed off the new Air Force One and defended the gift from the Qatari royal
family while campaigning for Republicans in Arizona today.
Trump was there to stump for Congressman Andy Biggs, the Republican candidate for governor
of the swing state.
Trump accepted the airplane gift last year despite criticism, including from some of
his staunchest allies. At the rally, he defended his decision by saying, "You take gifts when
they're given to you." Trump is now headed to Montana.
U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes and airfare has got more expensive.
As NPR's Scott Horsley explains, the figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran
War on gas prices as costs outpace wage gains.
Average wages have gone up just 3 percent over the last year, while prices have jumped
3.7 percent. So that means the typical paycheck buys less today than it did a year ago. And
no wonder many workers feel like they're falling behind.
It's a little different for retirees. We got word this morning that social security benefits
will go up 3.6 percent in January. That's an automatic cost of living adjustment, or
COLA, that's supposed to protect seniors from inflation.
NPR's Scott Horsley reporting minority leader Chuck Schumer and Senate Senator Alex Padilla
of California say more than 100 Democratic staff will fan out across the country as election
observers. The Senate's program mirrors a longstanding bipartisan program in the House,
as NPR's Eric McDaniel reports.
Democrats have been preparing for more than 100 different types of election threats, from
the possibility that the president will again declare elections fraudulent to National Guard
troops or ICE agents at the polls. The White House has said in statements to NPR that the
administration is working to protect the election and that federal agents won't be specifically
dispatched to polls.
The new election observer program is the most visible part of Senate Democrats' preparations.
The Senate Republican, who would be responsible for any GOP participation in the observer
program, didn't immediately return a request for comment. Eric McDaniel, NPR News, Washington.
The Vatican says Pope Leo celebrated mass at the hospital today, where he's recovering
from lung cancer surgery. NPR's Jason DeRose reports the church also provided a medical
update.
According to the Vatican, Pope Leo has undergone routine post-op blood tests and a chest X-ray.
He's also having respiratory therapy. Leo's been active in his first 18 months, teaching
on artificial intelligence, traveling to Africa and the Middle East, and speaking out on war
and immigration. Catholic Studies professor Susan Reynolds at Emory University says the
cancer might bring something more to his papacy.
He has made a profound impact on the global church, but in other ways it does seem like
he's only just beginning. So I imagine that this will perhaps ignite in him a certain
sense of urgency.
For instance, appointing Cardinals, the people who will someday elect the next pope. Jason
DeRose, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes had their worst day since July today. The S&P 500 fell more than
1%. This is NPR News.
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff says he never followed up on a student's report
of being gang-raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The admission came as faculty prepared
to debate a no-confidence resolution in administration. This week, Kotlikoff announced new restrictions
on frat parties and more involvement with state police.
AI is often associated with replacing white-collar jobs and even destroying humanity. But in
India, AI is being developed to replace industrial jobs, as NPR's Deah Hadid reports factory
workers are training their own replacements.
In a textile factory in the southern Indian town of Karoor, women pack aprons into plastic
packaging and record their every hand movement through a GoPro fastened on a headset. That
footage is called egocentric data. Developers need millions of hours of it to train AI robots.
Even as experts say, India is emerging as a key place to record egocentric data, they
say the development of AI robots will likely be deployed in countries where labor is more
expensive and power is cheaper. They say these women in factory jobs might be saved by the
fact that their labor is cheap. Most are paid around $100 a month, and power here is considered
expensive for now.
Deah Hadid, NPR News, Karoor, Tamil Nadu, India.
Gianni Infantino is about to face his biggest critics as president of FIFA, the governing
body for world soccer. Tomorrow, he chairs the first FIFA council session since his controversial
World Cup sell-off plan was revealed and quickly dropped. Infantino's ties to President Trump
and other ethical concerns are also on the agenda.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump shows off new Air Force One and defends Qatari jet gift while campaigning for Biggs in Arizona
U.S. inflation accelerates as gas, clothing, and airfare costs rise; wages lag prices
Social Security benefits to rise 3.6 percent in January through cost-of-living adjustment
Schumer and Padilla announce more than 100 Democratic staff as election observers nationwide
Pope Leo celebrates mass at hospital while recovering from lung cancer surgery, Vatican says
Major U.S. stock indexes post worst day since July, with S&P 500 down more than 1%
Cornell president admits never following up on student's gang-rape report; faculty weigh no-confidence vote
In India, factory workers record hand movements to train AI robots that could replace them
FIFA's Infantino faces critics at first council session since dropped World Cup sell-off plan
